He didn't argue.

He just nodded at the clerk like they'd already had the conversation a hundred times.

I was standing two people behind him, holding a bag of dog food and a quart of motor oil for our Buick, and I watched him slide that milk back into the cooler with the kind of care a man uses when he's pretending nothing is wrong.

My husband slid a jar of pickles across the kitchen table one Thursday morning last spring.

He set it down by my coffee, lid pointed up at me.

Then he went back to his eggs.

And he didn't say a word about it.

For 41 years, opening jars was his job.

I never asked him to make it his.

It was just the way our kitchen ran.

The garbage was his, the folding was mine.

So I looked at the jar a second.

Then I gave the lid a twist, and it went.

I set a pickle on his plate like it was nothing at all.

Neither of us mentioned it.

But I'd been married too long for a thing like that not to snag on
